   - `"supported"`: Numbers, sign, polarity, and substantive direction accurately reflect the paper's primary empirical finding.

raw_response.adversarial_critique: Table 4 (PDF p. 10, journal p. 89) evaluates two co-primary household WASH outcomes—water coverage and sewerage coverage—across four census periods and two functional forms (level change Δ and rate of change %Δ, 16 WASH specifications total, N = 564 matched municipalities: 418 treated, 146 control), creating substantial outcome and window multiplicity that makes a single-row SWiM direction genuinely defensible both ways. Household water coverage is statistically null in all 8 of 8 specifications (all |t| <= 0.894, including post-reform 1995–2005 Δ = .041, t = .836 and 2000–2010 Δ = .000, t = .006), and even within sewerage coverage, 5 of 8 specifications are statistically null (|t| <= 1.077), including the full 20-year 1990–2010 window (Δ = .04, t = .821; %Δ = .851, t = .285) and the 2000–2010 level change (Δ = .008, t = .371). Conversely, the immediate post-1995-reform decade (1995–2005) shows strongly positive, statistically significant sewerage gains in both levels (Δ = .086***, SE = .034, t = 2.55) and rate of change (%Δ = 9.05***, SE = 2.18, t = 4.15), alongside 2000–2010 sewerage rate of change (%Δ = 3.401***, SE = .871, t = 3.905), which substantiate Claude's Favourable coding for post-reform sanitation if chosen over the null water and full-period models, yet Claude left alternative_substantive_direction blank. In estimate_full, Claude also committed a clear table-reading error by reporting the 1990–2010 water level result as "ATT = 0.027, p=0.595", mistaking .595—which in Table 4 (PDF p. 10) is the t-statistic for the adjacent %Δ column (ATT = .17, SE = 0.285, t = .595)—for the p-value of the Δ column (ATT = .027, SE = 0.03, t = .893, two-sided p ≈ 0.37), while mislabelling the relative growth ratio 9.05 (%Δ) as a "percentage-point ATT" and not noting that t = 2.55 on .086*** corresponds to two-sided normal p ≈ 0.011 rather than < 0.01. Finally, while the Elsevier PDF text layer strips Unicode minus signs from negative table entries (demonstrated by Table 2 on PDF p. 8 and Table 5 on PDF p. 10), the prose on PDF p. 9 explicitly confirms the positive sign of the starred sewerage ATTs, and the dossier's automated author-mismatch flag is merely an artifact of the split acute accent in "DI´AZ-CAYEROS" on PDF p. 1.

However, three numerical/unit discrepancies appear: (1) in estimate_full, Claude reports piped-water "1990-2010 level ATT = 0.027, p=0.595", but Table 4 cells stack ATT, SE, and t-value vertically—for Water 1990–2010 Δ (level), ATT = .027, SE = 0.03, and t = .893 (two-sided p ≈ 0.372), whereas .595 is the t-value from the adjacent 1990–2010 %Δ column (ATT = .17, SE = 0.285, t = .595); (2) Claude describes 9.05 as a "9.05 percentage-point ATT in rate of change", whereas .086 (8.6 percentage points on a 0–1 proportion scale) is the percentage-point level change and 9.05 is the relative rate of change conditional on initial baseline levels (PDF p. 9); and (3) although Table 4 prints *** (defined as .01) on .086***, the reported t-value of 2.55 (0.086 / 0.034 = 2.53) yields a two-sided normal p-value of ~0.0108 (p < 0.05, borderline 0.01).
